sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Central Sector Schemes (CSS)**: Fully financed by the Union Government and implemented by Central Ministries/Agencies or Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs), primarily targeting subjects under the **Union List (List I)**.
• **Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS-sponsored)**: Jointly funded by the Centre and States (typically 60:40 for general states, 90:10 for North-Eastern and Himalayan states, and 100% for UTs without legislature) to execute initiatives in the **State List (List II)** or **Concurrent List (List III)**.
• **Rationalization & Subsumation**: Following the **Subba Rao Committee** and subsequent NITI Aayog recommendations (2015), schemes were restructured into Core Schemes, Core of the Core Schemes, and Optional Schemes.
• **Key Fiscal Mechanism**: Implementation through the **Public Financial Management System (PFMS)** and **Single Nodal Agency (SNA)** model to ensure just-in-time release of funds and prevent blocking of capital.

items.definition: A mechanism mandated by the Ministry of Finance where every state designates a single nodal bank account for a specific scheme to track fund flow and check idle float.
Transfer of subsidies and welfare payments directly to the Aadhaar-seeded bank accounts of beneficiaries, minimizing leakages and intermediaries.
Periodic committees (such as the Chaturvedi Committee or NITI Aayog sub-groups) aimed at reducing the proliferation of schemes into umbrella programs.
Platform where Chief Ministers and Lieutenant Governors deliberate on scheme rationalization, performance monitoring, and cooperative federalism.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **North-Eastern & Himalayan States**: Benefit from the favorable 90:10 funding ratio under Centrally Sponsored Schemes to bridge infrastructural and developmental deficits.
• **Aspirational Districts Programme (ADP) / Aspirational Blocks**: Spatial targeting of CSS allocations to lagging districts based on multi-dimensional health, education, and economic indicators.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Delays in state-share release, rigid central guidelines ignoring local topography, compliance burdens, and idle fund accumulation in commercial banks.
• **Policy Interventions**: Adoption of the SNA-Sparsh framework, outcome-based budgeting, third-party evaluations by DMEO (Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office).

items.title: Mnemonic for Centrally Sponsored Funding Ratios
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: 'GEN-64, NE-91, UT-100'
• **Decoded Meaning**: General States = 60:40 (Centre:State); North-Eastern/Himalayan = 90:10; Union Territories without legislature = 100% Central.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly eliminates incorrect funding ratio options in matching-list questions.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: 'Central Sector = Union List & 100% Central; Centrally Sponsored = State/Concurrent List & Shared Funding'.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that 'All welfare schemes implemented in states are Centrally Sponsored Schemes.' This is false; schemes like PM-KISAN and Railways projects are Central Sector Schemes entirely funded by the Centre.

Mains Value Addition: In GS-2 (Federalism) or GS-3 (Inclusive Growth), argue how excessive conditionalities in Centrally Sponsored Schemes undermine fiscal federalism, and quote the 14th/15th Finance Commission recommendations on optimal tax devolution versus tied grants.

keyTakeaways: Central Sector Schemes are 100% funded by the Union Government, while Centrally Sponsored Schemes involve cost-sharing between Centre and States.
The introduction of the Single Nodal Agency (SNA) model has revolutionized fund tracking and eliminated idle float in scheme execution.
UPSC tests conceptual clarity regarding funding ratios (60:40, 90:10) and jurisdictional distribution under the Seventh Schedule.
